title: Who are mandatory reporters of child abuse in Australian healthcare, and what training is required?
seoTitle: Child abuse mandatory reporting by state
description: Which health workers must report child abuse in NSW, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia and WA, the legal thresholds, and the training NSW Health mandates.
shortAnswer: Every Australian state makes doctors and nurses mandatory reporters of child abuse, but the threshold differs. In Victoria, doctors, nurses and midwives must report a reasonable belief of physical or sexual abuse. Queensland requires doctors and registered nurses to report a reasonable suspicion of significant harm from physical or sexual abuse. South Australia covers a wider group, including pharmacists and dentists. NSW Health policy makes two hours of child protection training a core requirement for all health workers.
keyTakeaways: Reporting duties are set by state law, not national law: Victoria (section 184, Children, Youth and Families Act 2005), Queensland (section 13E, Child Protection Act 1999), South Australia (section 31, Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017) and NSW (section 27, Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998).

Thresholds vary: belief on reasonable grounds in Victoria, reasonable suspicion of significant harm in Queensland, suspicion on reasonable grounds of risk in South Australia, and risk of significant harm in NSW.
Western Australia's duty covers child sexual abuse only, and its reporter list includes doctors, nurses, midwives and psychologists.

NSW Health policy directive PD2013_007 sets two hours of core child protection training at induction for all health workers and at least one day of face to face training for those working with children or with parents whose capacity may be in question.
Most statutes do not themselves prescribe training, so a training program has to be built around each state's reporter list, threshold and reporting channel.
jurisdiction: Australia (New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia)
regulator: State child protection agencies: the Secretary (Victoria), the chief executive (Queensland), the Child Abuse Report Line (South Australia), the Child Protection Helpline (NSW) and the Department of Communities (Western Australia), under each state's child protection Act
appliesTo: Registered medical practitioners and nurses in every state covered on this page
Midwives in Victoria and Western Australia
Pharmacists, dentists, enrolled nurses and psychologists in South Australia
Hospitals, health services and clinics that employ mandatory reporters and design their child protection training

sections.heading: Which health workers are mandatory reporters in each state?

blocks.text: Doctors and nurses are mandatory reporters in all five states covered here, but the list of other health professions, the type of harm and the threshold for reporting differ by state. The table summarizes the provisions read on each state's official legislation site or government page. The Northern Territory, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory are not covered because they were not verified for this page.

blocks.title: Currency and transition
blocks.text: This page reflects the legislation and state guidance as at November 2026. Victorian provisions were read in version 149 of the Act, effective September 30, 2026. South Australia's 2017 Act is marked for repeal by the Children and Young People (Safety and Support) Act 2025, which had not replaced it in the authorized current version at the time of checking, so South Australian services should watch for the commencement date.

sections.heading: What does Victoria require of doctors, nurses and midwives?

blocks.text: Victorian doctors, nurses and midwives must report to the Secretary when, in the course of their work, they form a belief on reasonable grounds that a child needs protection from physical injury or sexual abuse. Section 182 of the [Children, Youth and Families Act 2005](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/children-youth-and-families-act-2005) lists "a registered medical practitioner", "a nurse" and "a midwife" as mandatory reporters.

Section 184(1) ties the duty to the grounds in section 162(1)(c) and (d), significant harm from physical injury or sexual abuse where the parents have not protected or are unlikely to protect the child. The report must be made as soon as practicable after forming the belief and again each time further reasonable grounds arise. The maximum penalty is 10 penalty units, and section 184(4) measures reasonableness against a reasonable person in the same profession. Section 184(2A) states that privilege under section 127 of the Evidence Act 2008 does not remove the duty.

sections.heading: How do Queensland and South Australia differ?

blocks.text: Queensland's duty is narrower in professions covered, while South Australia's reaches a wider group of health workers and a lower threshold. Under section 13E of the [Child Protection Act 1999](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/act-1999-010), doctors and registered nurses who form a reportable suspicion in the course of their work must give a written report to the chief executive. Section 13G says the report must state the basis for the suspicion and the prescribed information, and need not be given if the person knows or reasonably supposes the chief executive is already aware of the matter.

In South Australia, section 30 of the [Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017](https://www.legislation.sa.gov.au/_legislation-documents/lz/c/a/children-and-young-people-safety-act-2017/current/2017.25.auth.pdf) defines prescribed health practitioners as medical practitioners, pharmacists, registered or enrolled nurses, dentists and psychologists. Section 31 requires them to report a suspicion on reasonable grounds that a child is or may be at risk as soon as reasonably practicable, with a maximum penalty of $10,000. Reports go through the Child Abuse Report Line, an electronic system the Minister determines, or another channel the Act allows. Students on practical placements count as employed for this purpose under section 30(4).

sections.heading: What applies to health workers in NSW and Western Australia?

blocks.text: NSW Health workers must report a child under 16 they suspect is at risk of significant harm under section 27 of the Care Act, using the Mandatory Reporter Guide to judge the threshold. The [NSW Health child protection policy directive (PD2013_007)](https://www1.health.nsw.gov.au/pds/ActivePDSDocuments/PD2013_007.pdf) also allows reporting to the NSW Health Child Wellbeing Unit under section 27A in appropriate cases and requires services to protect reporter identity under section 29. NSW Health's [child protection page](https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/parvan/childprotect/Pages/default.aspx) notes that prenatal reports are permitted but not mandatory.

NSW also created separate criminal offenses in the Crimes Act 1900 from August 31, 2018: concealing a child abuse offense (section 316A) and failing to remove the risk that a worker will commit a child abuse offense (section 43B). NSW Health says a report already made under mandatory reporting obligations is a reasonable excuse for not also reporting to police.

In Western Australia, the [Department of Communities guidance](https://www.wa.gov.au/service/community-services/community-support/mandatory-reporting-of-child-sexual-abuse-wa) explains that the duty applies to child sexual abuse only. A report may be made orally or in writing, but an oral report must be followed by a written one as soon as practicable, ideally within 24 hours. Concerns about physical or emotional abuse or neglect go through a separate professional referral form.

sections.heading: Is mandatory reporting training itself mandatory?

blocks.text: The statutes covered here impose the duty to report but do not themselves prescribe a training course, so training obligations come from employer policy. NSW Health is the clearest example. PD2013_007 makes local health districts and specialty networks responsible for providing mandatory child protection training and states that "Two hours training is a core training requirement for all health workers", delivered as part of induction.

The same directive says health workers working directly with children, including maternity, child and youth health and pediatric services, or with adults whose parenting capacity may be in question, such as mental health and drug and alcohol services, should attend at least one day of face to face training at orientation or soon after. Staff who deliver this training should complete Child Protection Facilitator training through the Education Centre Against Violence. The directive was issued in April 2013 and remains listed as active even though its stated review date of February 28, 2021 has passed.

Western Australia offers free Mandatory Reporting Online Training for existing and new reporter groups, in three parts of two modules each with a short quiz, taking up to two hours and generating a completion certificate. The state's guidance presents it as available rather than legally required. WA phased in new reporter groups over three years to 2025 specifically so they could be trained before the duty applied, and the expansion is now complete.

sections.heading: How should a health service map duties to roles, frequency and evidence?

blocks.text: A multistate health provider needs a training plan that reflects each state's reporter list and threshold rather than one national module. The mapping below is original and illustrative, built from the provisions above. It is not endorsed by any state agency. The broader method is explained in the [obligation mapping guide](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats each state's reporter categories, harm types and thresholds as separate concepts and links them to the roles a provider employs in that state. A clinician who moves from Brisbane to Adelaide can then be assessed only on what differs, such as the broader South Australian threshold, instead of repeating a generic module.

faqs.q: Are pharmacists mandatory reporters of child abuse?
faqs.a: In South Australia, yes. Section 30(5) of the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 lists pharmacists as prescribed health practitioners who must report. They are not named in the Victorian or Queensland provisions covered here, although general duties and employer policies may still apply.

faqs.q: Does a nurse who moves interstate need new training?
faqs.a: The reporter list, threshold and reporting channel change across state lines, so a nurse should be trained on the rules where they practice. For example, Queensland requires a written report about physical or sexual abuse, while South Australia requires a report of any reasonable suspicion of risk.

faqs.q: Is reporting required for unborn children?
faqs.a: Generally no. NSW permits but does not require prenatal reports, and section 31(3) of the South Australian Act says a person may, but need not, report a suspicion that an unborn child's development is at risk.

faqs.q: What happens if a mandatory reporter fails to report?
faqs.a: Penalties differ by state. Victoria sets a maximum of 10 penalty units under section 184, and South Australia a maximum of $10,000 under section 31. Professional consequences through registration bodies may also follow.

faqs.q: Does patient confidentiality override the duty to report?
faqs.a: No. NSW Health policy states that client confidentiality is not a sufficient reason against reporting, and Victoria's Act states that privilege under section 127 of the Evidence Act 2008 does not exempt a reporter.
